To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) The organization of multiple functional brain networks shifts from a more anatomical emphasis in young children to a more “distributed” architecture in young adults; (2) The graphs representing the connectivity of multiple functional networks show “small-world” properties in both young children and adults; (3) Communities within these graphs, as defined by modularity optimization, show different patterns in children and adults; and (4) In sum, these results provide evidence for a “local to distributed” developmental trajectory

the organization of functional connectivity networks in the developing brain shifts from a local to distributed architecture, and this shift is associated with the emergence of communities that reflect functional rather than purely anatomical relationships.
functional brain networks develop from a local anatomically defined organization to a more distributed organization in adulthood.
